President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".

The company published its latest threat intelligence report, external on Thursday.

Such reports have become a regular feature across the AI industry as firms seek to demonstrate how they identify and disrupt attempts to misuse their models.

This includes Google, which wrote on Tuesday, external that a person had attempted to use its AI tool, Gemini, to obtain a "complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponised biological agents".

Claude, Anthropic's AI model was also used by actors linked to a Russia-based cyber espionage campaign and by an Iranian propaganda institution, according to its report.

The cases of concern detected over the past eight months ranged from fake dating apps and hotel Wifi scams, to surveillance built to identify dissidents.

Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI firms of trying to replicate Claude's capabilities.

The lengthy report lists cases in which suspected state-sponsored groups, criminals, spyware vendors, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals misused its technology.

"Malicious use" of its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models was disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, it said.

None of the misuse cases involved Claude Fable or the powerful Mythos-class models, with the exception of one instance of distillation - the process for training smaller AI models using larger, more expensive models.

As well as detecting the use of its models for cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud and weapon development, Anthropic said it had blocked scientists who used its AI in ways that could support biological weapons development.

The report highlighted "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development".

Biological misuse, it said, is "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI model". Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities "could have catastrophic consequences", Anthropic said.

"The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," Anthropic said.

Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told the New York Times, external it was "an incredibly nuanced situation".

At the time both the CIA and the FBI were in possession of information which, if shared properly, could have prevented what happened.

The 9/11 Commission Report that followed blamed "failures of imagination, policy, capabilities and management" on the US government. The CIA and FBI, the report concluded, failed to properly assess intelligence and share information with each other and take sufficient steps to disrupt the plot.

This most basic of lessons has since been largely – although not completely – learnt, and sharing between Western intelligence agencies is infinitely better than it was in 2001.

The old rivalries between say, MI5 and Police Counter Terrorism have dissolved, first with regional 'fusion centres' dotted around the UK and now, most recently, with the establishment of the high-security Counter Terrorism Operations Centre in London. Here MI5 intelligence officers might find themselves sitting literally right next to police officers whose job it is to take the executive action to stop a terrorist plot. Equally, they might find themselves sitting next to a US federal agent from the FBI or a language specialist seconded from GCHQ.

Since 9/11, there has also been a root-and-branch reorganisation of US intelligence with the establishment of a National Counter Terrorism Center just outside Washington DC and a Director of National Intelligence to ensure that information is shared where it needs to be between the 18 separate US intelligence agencies. The relationship between the CIA and its UK counterpart, the Secret Intelligence Service (better known as MI6) is perhaps the closest one in the world. This is supplemented by the Five Eyes alliance that pools intelligence between the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

Yet disastrous failures of intelligence, assessment and strategic planning have still occurred since the planes hit the Twin Towers. Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory.

Fighting decreased following a ceasefire deal between Iran and the US in June, alongside a separate agreement between Lebanon and Israel.

Under the Lebanon-Israel framework, Hezbollah is expected to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.

Hezbollah was not directly involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations.

Despite a reduction in fighting, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued.

At least 4,362 people have been killed in Lebanon during the conflict, including 395 women and 259 children, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians.

Nigeria's ride-hailing economics under pressure

Competition gives drivers more options

Uganda had its own fight

Uber becomes selective in Africa

Uber is pulling out of Nigeria and Uganda, closing operations in two African markets where ride-hailing companies have faced a difficult combination of rising operating costs, pressure on fares and growing competition.The exits took effect on September 2, ending Uber's 12-year run in Nigeria and roughly a decade in Uganda. The company said it reached the “difficult decision” after a “thorough review” of its business priorities, while stressing that the move applies only to the two countries.“This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent,” Uber told BBC.“We remain committed to sub-Saharan Africa, where we continue to see strong growth and opportunity.”For Uber, Nigeria had been more than just a conventional ride-hailing market. The company entered the country in 2014 and expanded its services over the following years, including launching a boat service in Lagos in 2019 to help commuters avoid the city's notorious traffic.But the economics of driving for ride-hailing platforms have become increasingly difficult.Uber drivers in Nigeria have complained that fares on the app are too low as fuel and other operating costs rise, while commissions charged by platforms are too high.The wider industry has faced similar pressure. Drivers working for Uber, Bolt and inDrive staged a three-day strike in Lagos and Ogun in March over what they described as unsustainable fares and poor working conditions.The cost pressures have intensified following economic changes in Nigeria. The removal of the fuel subsidy after President Bola Tinubu's election in 2023 pushed up the cost of living, while petrol prices rose again this year following the US's war with Iran.For drivers, the pressure extends beyond fuel. Petrol, imported spare parts and vehicle maintenance have all become more expensive, squeezing incomes while fares remain under pressure.Uber has also had to operate in a market where passengers and drivers have an expanding choice of platforms.Bolt and inDrive are major competitors in Nigeria, while local services include Rida and LagRide. inDrive allows passengers and drivers to negotiate fares, and its global model has generally involved a service fee of about 10%.The ability of drivers to move between platforms, or leave ride-hailing altogether, provides an alternative when commissions or fares become unattractive.That creates a difficult equation for platforms as operating costs increase. A large customer base may generate plenty of rides without necessarily producing enough margin.The pressures were different in Uganda but centred on a similar issue: the ability of drivers and platforms to make the business work.Uber entered Uganda in 2016 and later introduced UberBODA. But its commission structure had already faced resistance from drivers.In 2019, the Smart Online Drivers Association petitioned parliament over what it described as exploitative practices. Drivers were particularly concerned about Uber's 25% commission while fares remained low.By the time Uber announced its departure, Kampala already had established alternatives. Bolt and SafeBoda were competing with Uber, while smaller platforms including Faras, Yango and Tinka had added to the competition.Uganda's Daily Monitor said Uber's departure would bring a major change for commuters in Kampala, but that other taxi apps such as Faras, Bolt and SafeBoda were likely to fill the gap.Nigeria and Uganda are not the first African markets Uber has left.The company exited Ivory Coast last year after six years of operations and ended its Tanzania service in January this year after nearly a decade. The latest departures leave Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa as the only African countries where Uber operates, BBC reported.The company has pledged to support employees and drivers affected by the closures. Its help centre will remain available to users in Nigeria and Uganda until September 23 to resolve outstanding issues.The departures also come as Uber chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi announced a 10% cut to the company's global workforce, with more than 3,000 jobs affected in a major restructuring.For the ride-hailing business in Nigeria and Uganda, the issue is not simply whether passengers are available. Platforms have to contend with the competing demands of keeping fares affordable, ensuring drivers can earn enough and maintaining commissions that make the business worthwhile.Uber's latest exits leave it with a smaller footprint in Africa, even as the company says it continues to see strong growth and opportunity in sub-Saharan Africa.platforms nigeria market business tougher ridehailing drivers africa uber uganda company exits africas fares gettingIn the 1950s, Hugo Meyer began buying abandoned Vermont farmland to grow timber; his family has now helped permanently protect more than 18,000 acres from developmentA history of sustainable timber management

A vital natural corridor

Growing up in Hardwick on a dairy farm, woods were a major part of Andrew Meyer's life. He would often spend time camping and hiking around East Long Pond and as a kid, he visited logging jobs in the area of the Worcester Range with his grandfather or uncle.Meyer said his family’s been managing the woods as a working forest since the 1950s, when his grandfather started purchasing land in the region. Hugo Meyer began buying abandoned farmland after World War II to reforest it for timber. In the decades since, the family has owned and managed thousands of acres in and around the Worcester Range, maintaining the land as a working forest. As pressures on land have increased over recent decades, the family felt conservation offered a way to keep the property together and support continued family ownership and sustainable management.“These forests have been part of our family’s story for generations,” said landowner Andrew Meyer. “Conservation offers a way to keep the land together while continuing the stewardship and sustainable forestry practices that have shaped it over the years. We’re proud to be part of an effort that protects the character of this landscape, supports our continued management of this working forest, and helps ensure that future generations can benefit from the same connection to the land that our family has had.The conserved land includes extensive and varied forest habitat and wetlands, as well as a mile of undeveloped shoreline along East Long Pond. The property has been actively managed for timber for decades and will remain a working forest under the conservation easement. Forest Legacy easements are specifically designed to prevent fragmentation and development while allowing sustainable forestry to continue.Over the years, E.B. Hyde Corp., Meyer's family-run timber company, worked for more than a decade with several partner organisations to bring more than 18,000 acres under conservation easements. In August 2026, they finalised the last of the three phases of the Worcester Woods project, placing more than 3,400 acres into an easement. The project involves a partnership among the Vermont Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation, the Vermont Land Trust and the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department, along with other partners. Much of the funding for this project came from the U.S. Forest Service’s Forest Legacy Program. That’s revenue that comes partly from leasing federal offshore oil and gas sites.According to Kate Sudhoff, a land conservation manager at the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation, what has been conserved by Meyers' family is an important wildlife corridor, a contiguous tract that animals can use to travel across the landscape. It is home to loons and some rare plants and flowers, and there’s a mile of lake frontage on East Long Pond. Its main ecological value, though, is that it’s an intact northern hardwood forest, an important habitat for wildlife in the state. It’s also a high-priority conservation area for the Vermont Agency of Natural Resources. “This one, we always thought of as the gem,” Sudhoff said.“It requires a very patient landowner,” she said, noting it can take years for everything to be finalised. “They have to be really willing and interested in selling these rights and holding the land. And the landowner’s interest in the land has to align with the program.” Meyer is very patient as a landowner. He said trees take 80 years to grow, and he manages his forests in 20- and 30-year cycles. “You have to think long term because these trees take so long to grow, and the health of the forest is critical to that,” he said.For him, the permanent easement will allow the opportunity to think about the future of the land more easily. He doesn't have to worry about development pressure or policy changes ever. “The understanding that that’s really part of the legacy of what my grandfather had envisioned and set forth over 70 years ago,” he said.Easement purchases are a conservation tool where the land remains in private ownership, but the landowner is bound to the restrictions and agreements that come with the easement. For example, easements involving the Department of Forests, Parks and Recreation require that the area be publicly accessible and open for hunting.Will Duane is the land acquisition coordinator with Vermont Fish & Wildlife. He said that even if the landowner decides to sell the land, the easement remains, and the public rights go along with the property. “We’re paying the landowners,” he said. “They’re keeping the land private, but they’re selling some of those land rights to us to conserve it and to bring the public onto it.”The land can’t be subdivided and developed, and an appraisal process determines the difference in value between what the owners might make from selling and developing the land instead of keeping it in conservation. They’re selling those rights, which cost a little less than $5 million for the final phase of the Worcester Woods project.Vermont Fish & Wildlife also purchased from the Meyer family a 301-acre parcel that will become part of the Buck Lake Wildlife Management Area. That expanded the footprint of the Green Mountain Conservation Camp, a popular and affordable summer camp in the wildlife management area where kids can learn outdoor skills and natural science. “It’s a real win-win-win across the board,” Duane said.Meyer now plans to sustainably log the Worcester Woods for many generations. “This is such a big, important piece of land in our region that so many people enjoy,” he said. “Whether they’re the logger cutting the wood, or the hunter or the hiker, or just knowing there are large parcels of contiguous land around them is what makes this region of Vermont so special. “We’re obligated to recognise that and be in the position to help keep that the way it is, and a lot of people are going to benefit from that. ”Beyond Vermont’s borders, scientists and conservation organisations have long recognised Worcester Woods as a critical link for climate resilience and wildlife movement. In 2012, the Staying Connected Initiative highlighted the Worcester Range as the “linchpin” connecting larger forest landscapes across northern New England and southeastern Canada.land grow timber helped conservation permanently worcester family wildlife woods landowner forest long vermont hugo meyer protect farmlandAfter over 75% of Niagara River coastal wetlands were lost, Canada anchored recycled Christmas trees into the riverbed; restoration has now created 1.64 km of fish habitatRepresentative Image (AI-generated)

Why the loss of wetlands mattered

How old Christmas trees became fish habitat

Building a more natural shoreline

A restoration project with wider benefits

What if a discarded Christmas tree could help bring a damaged river ecosystem back to life? For years, the Niagara River’s shoreline has been losing an important part of its natural ecosystem. More than 75% of the original coastal wetlands on the Canadian side had disappeared, reducing the shallow, sheltered areas that fish need for feeding, breeding and growing. In response, conservation teams began using an unusual but practical material: dead trees, including recycled Christmas trees, anchored directly into the riverbed. The structures help slow waves, reduce erosion and create calmer areas where aquatic life can thrive.According to Niagara Parks, the coastal wetland restoration programme began in 2016 in partnership with the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry and Environment and Climate Change Canada. The programme was designed to restore shoreline habitat at strategic locations along the Niagara River. A 2025-26 Niagara Parks sustainability report says that 1.64 kilometres of habitat structure have now been installed in the Upper Niagara River, with additional work continuing at sites including Black Creek and Boyer’s Creek.Coastal wetlands are much more than strips of vegetation along a river. They provide sheltered, shallow-water environments that can serve as nursery habitat for young fish. When these areas disappear, species lose places where they can feed, reproduce and find protection from stronger currents. According to Niagara Parks, the loss of more than three-quarters of the original coastal wetlands had removed important fish nursery habitat and severely affected species including lake sturgeon and muskellunge. The restoration programme therefore focuses not only on stopping shoreline erosion but also on rebuilding the physical conditions needed for aquatic life. The approach is relatively simple. Instead of relying entirely on new manufactured structures, conservation workers have reused natural materials that would otherwise have been discarded or chipped.One of the most distinctive parts of the project involved recycled Christmas trees. Niagara Parks anchored trees into the riverbed, where they act as underwater structures that interrupt wave energy and create calmer conditions near the shore. The idea is to recreate some of the complexity that naturally fallen trees can provide in waterways. Branches and trunks create physical cover and additional surfaces in the water, potentially giving fish and other aquatic organisms places to shelter.At Boyer’s Creek in 2019, Niagara Parks planned to repurpose a roughly 30-foot blue spruce that had been displayed in Queen Victoria Park during the holiday season. Rather than sending the tree for disposal, the park intended to use it as anchoring material in the riverbed. The programme has also made use of ash trees affected by the emerald ash borer. Rather than simply removing and disposing of these dead trees, some have been incorporated into shoreline restoration projects.The restoration effort has expanded beyond Christmas trees. Niagara Parks has also experimented with anchoring fallen ash trees to their remaining stumps so they can rest on the riverbed, imitating the way trees naturally fall into waterways. These structures can provide what conservationists call instant fish habitat while also helping protect the shoreline. Riparian zones, where land meets water, can provide food and shelter for aquatic organisms, regulate water temperatures and help resist erosion.The programme has grown considerably since the early projects. Niagara Parks' latest sustainability report says 1.64 kilometres of habitat structure have now been installed in the Upper Niagara River. In summer 2025, crews added structures at the mouths of Black Creek and Boyer’s Creek, including 70 tree and log structures and more than 360 tonnes of boulders. Together, that work created approximately 240 metres of additional coastal wetland habitat.The results are intended to extend beyond shoreline protection. Niagara Parks reports that restoration efforts have already been associated with increased fish and shorebird populations and greater diversity, along with improved water quality at restored sites. What began as an effort to repair a heavily altered shoreline has therefore developed into a broader ecological restoration programme. By turning unwanted trees into structures that resemble natural river habitat, conservationists are giving the Niagara River's shoreline another chance to function more like a living ecosystem.The unusual use of recycled Christmas trees is a reminder that restoration does not always require entirely new materials. Sometimes, discarded parts of the landscape can become the building blocks for bringing damaged habitats back to life.riverbed recycled structures restoration trees programme lost parks shoreline niagara river habitat km wetlands fishA former AT&T worker used employee access for SIM swaps; prosecutors say the conspiracy tried to steal nearly $600,000 from victims’ bank accountsRepresentative image

How

SIM swapping

works

The alleged role of the former employee

Nearly $600,000 in intended losses

Evidence found during the investigation

A breach of trust

Why text message security can fail

The lasting lesson

A cellphone number can appear to be a simple way to reach someone, but it is also often tied to bank accounts, password resets and two factor authentication. Federal prosecutors say a former AT&T retail employee exploited that connection by helping a hacker transfer customers’ phone numbers to devices controlled by criminals. The scheme allegedly gave co conspirators access to victims’ banking information and enabled fraudulent wire transfers. Three identified victims faced a combined intended loss of at least $593,963, according to court records and the US Department of Justice. As reported by AOL, former Oregon AT&T worker Kenneth Carter was sentenced to 16 months in federal prison and ordered to pay $99,528 in restitution after pleading guilty to conspiracy charges.A SIM swap occurs when a mobile phone number is moved from the legitimate customer’s SIM card to a different SIM card controlled by someone else. Once the transfer is completed, calls and text messages intended for the victim can reach the criminal’s device instead.That can be especially damaging when a bank sends password reset links or security codes by text message. If a criminal already has personal information about the account holder, control of the phone number may provide the final step needed to enter an online bank account.The attacker can then change passwords, intercept verification messages and attempt to move money.SIM swapping does not necessarily require sophisticated hacking in the traditional sense. Often, the criminal relies on social engineering, stolen personal information or help from someone inside a telecommunications company. An employee with access to customer accounts may be able to make changes that an ordinary outsider could not.That insider access is what made the alleged scheme particularly serious. According to prosecutors, Carter did not merely provide information. He used his position at an AT&T store to carry out unauthorised changes on customer accounts.Carter, 44, of Portland, Oregon, worked at an AT&T retail store from May 2018 through November 2019. Prosecutors said a co-conspirator identified potential victims, gathered personal identifying information and sent the details to Carter along with the victims’ cellphone numbers.Carter then allegedly used his employee access to cause AT&T to transfer each victim’s number from the legitimate SIM card to another phone controlled by him or his co conspirators. The criminals could then receive texts and calls meant for the account holder.The co-conspirator allegedly used that control to obtain password reset information and two-factor authentication codes for online bank accounts. Those details were then passed to another participant, who accessed the accounts and arranged fraudulent wire transfers.The indictment and plea materials describe a division of labour. One person gathered information, Carter performed the telecommunications changes and other conspirators used the stolen access to target bank accounts. Prosecutors said Carter and others typically received between $1,000 and $2,000 for each SIM swap.The case involved at least three identified victims, who prosecutors said faced a combined intended loss of $593,963. One victim had nearly $100,000 transferred to a Portuguese bank account controlled by co-conspirators. Carter was ordered to pay $99,528 in restitution connected to that loss.The term “intended loss” is important in federal cases. It refers to the amount the conspirators sought or attempted to steal, not necessarily the amount that successfully left every victim’s account. Prosecutors said fraud prevention systems at some banks stopped additional transfers before the money could be wired overseas.The alleged losses demonstrate why control of a mobile phone number can be so valuable to criminals. A phone number may serve as a gateway to accounts containing far more money than the cost of a phone plan or SIM card. Once the criminal intercepts security messages, the victim may find that familiar protections work against them.The victim may still have a working phone, but it suddenly loses service when the number is transferred. In other cases, the change may not be immediately noticed, giving attackers time to reset passwords and initiate transfers.In November 2019, law enforcement searched Carter’s Oregon residence and found personal identifying information connected to victims, according to prosecutors. The materials included names, cellphone numbers and Social Security numbers.The discovery helped connect the employee’s access to the broader conspiracy. Carter later admitted that he performed SIM swaps involving other AT&T customers beyond the three victims whose intended losses were detailed in the case.The investigation involved several federal agencies, including the FBI, the FDIC Office of Inspector General and IRS Criminal Investigation. Their involvement reflected the case’s overlap between telecommunications fraud, identity theft and bank fraud.After the investigation, Carter pleaded guilty on March 24, 2026, to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and bank fraud. A federal judge later sentenced him to 16 months in prison and ordered restitution, as per the report.Prosecutors described the conduct as an abuse of employer trust. Carter’s access existed so he could serve legitimate customers, but authorities said he sold that access to a hacker and used it to redirect customers’ phone numbers.The case highlights a difficult security problem for telecommunications companies. Employees need enough access to resolve account issues, activate devices and make authorised changes. At the same time, that access can become dangerous if internal controls are weak or if employees cooperate with criminals.Companies can reduce the risk through stronger identity verification, detailed audit logs, limits on employee privileges and alerts for unusual account changes. A SIM transfer involving a high value customer account or a recent password reset may deserve additional review. Employee training and background checks can also play a role, although no single measure eliminates insider threats.For customers, the incident is a reminder that mobile carrier accounts should be treated as part of financial security, not merely as communication services.Many people use text messages for two-factor authentication because they are convenient. A code sent by text is safer than a password alone, but it depends on the phone number remaining under the customer’s control. A successful SIM swap breaks that assumption.Security specialists often recommend using an authentication app or a physical security key for important accounts when those options are available. Customers can also ask their carrier about account PINs, port out protections and alerts for SIM changes. These controls may make it harder for an attacker to move a number without the account holder’s knowledge.No security method is perfect, especially when criminals possess personal information from data breaches or social media. However, using stronger authentication can reduce the damage if a phone number is stolen.Customers should also respond quickly to warning signs. Sudden loss of mobile service, unexpected password reset messages, banking alerts or unfamiliar transactions should be treated seriously. Contacting the mobile carrier and financial institution through verified channels can help limit further loss.The alleged scheme shows how cybercrime can combine human access with ordinary digital tools. The criminals did not need to break through every layer of a bank’s security system if they could first take control of the victim’s phone number. An insider at a telecommunications store made that step possible.For the victims, the consequences extended beyond financial loss. A stolen phone number can expose private messages, disrupt access to email and social accounts, and create weeks or months of recovery work. For employers, the case demonstrates why access must be monitored even when employees are authorised to use the system.Carter’s sentence closes one part of the case, but the broader risk remains. As more financial services rely on mobile numbers for identity verification, SIM swapping will continue to attract criminals. The best defence combines carrier safeguards, stronger account authentication, bank fraud monitoring and careful protection of personal information.say tried swaps bank worker accounts phone prosecutors number access account victims steal information security nearly used simWhile surveying a California creek for threatened red-legged frogs, a scientist spotted what looked like a rock; it was an intact mastodon molar estimated to be 10,000 years oldScientist finds 10,000-year-old mastodon molar while surveying California creek for threatened frogs (Image Credit: Balance Hydrologics)

From a strange-looking rock to an Ice Age fossil

The fossil is estimated to be at least 10,000 years old (Image Credit: Midpeninsula Open Space District)

A giant herbivore from California's past

What the tooth could reveal

A routine field survey in a California redwood forest has led to an extraordinary glimpse into the Ice Age. A scientist searching a San Mateo County creek for signs of habitat conditions for threatened California red-legged frogs spotted an oddly shaped object that initially appeared to be an ordinary rock. Instead, it turned out to be a remarkably well-preserved tooth belonging to an extinct Pacific mastodon. The fossil is estimated to be at least 10,000 years old and is being described as an exceptionally complete specimen from the region.According to the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen), geomorphologist Brigid Lynch discovered the fossil while working on a habitat enhancement project for California red-legged frogs. Paleontologists later confirmed that the object was an intact molar from an adult Pacific mastodon, a giant herbivore that once roamed parts of western North America.Lynch, who works with Balance Hydrologics, was surveying a creek bed when she noticed the unusual object. Its shape was distinctive enough to catch her attention, but there was initially no indication that it had survived from a prehistoric animal.Paleontologists later examined the object and identified it as a molar from a Pacific mastodon. The condition of the fossil made the discovery particularly significant. Wayne Thompson, a paleontologist and owner of Pacific Paleontology, described it as the most complete mastodon molar from the area and among the most impressive he had seen.The exact location of the discovery has not been disclosed. Midpen officials said the information was being kept private partly to prevent people from attempting to search the area themselves for fossils.The fossil belonged to Mammut pacificus, commonly known as the Pacific mastodon. Although mastodons are often associated with the better-known American mastodon, scientists recognise the Pacific mastodon as a distinct species. The species was formally recognised in 2019 following research on mastodon remains from Southern California. Pacific mastodons differed from American mastodons in several physical characteristics, including narrower teeth, thicker leg bones and differences in their tusks.These animals were large herbivores that lived during the Pleistocene, an epoch that began roughly 2.5 million years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. They ranged across parts of western North America, with Pacific mastodon remains identified in California, Idaho, Oregon and, more recently, parts of Mexico. Unlike mammoths, which primarily grazed on grasses, mastodons were browsers that fed on leaves, shoots and other vegetation. That makes the newly discovered tooth more than just an unusual fossil. It is a physical remnant of a landscape that existed thousands of years before modern California took shape.The fossil has now been donated to Stanford University's Doerr School of Sustainability for further study. Researchers plan to use carbon dating to determine its precise age rather than relying solely on the current estimate of at least 10,000 years. Scientists also intend to create a three-dimensional scan of the tooth. Midpen plans to use the resulting digital model and a replica for educational and public outreach purposes.According to the researchers, fossils such as this can help reconstruct past ecosystems and biodiversity. By studying what lived in a region thousands of years ago, scientists can gain a better understanding of how landscapes and species have changed over time. The discovery also creates an unexpected link between modern conservation and ancient history. Lynch was searching the landscape to support the habitat of a threatened frog species when she encountered evidence of an animal that disappeared thousands of years ago.For a moment, the creek bed offered a glimpse of a very different California, one where enormous mastodons moved through forests and other now-extinct animals shared the landscape. Today, that same environment is being studied and protected for species that are still here, making the accidental discovery a reminder of how dramatically ecosystems can change over time.molar fossil discovery old california mastodons pacific scientist species redlegged rock spotted tooth mastodon surveying looked object threatenedIn 1902, Hawaii introduced red mangroves to stabilize shorelines; 124 years later, the invasive trees clog waterways and degrade habitat used by endangered native waterbirdsRepresentative image of Hawaii from Canva

A solution imported from elsewhere

How red mangroves spread

A threat to native waterbirds

What the USGS research contributes

The cost of an old decision

Hawaii’s response

A lesson in ecological humility

Restoring space for native birds

In 1902, red mangroves were brought to Hawaii with an apparently practical purpose. Their tangled roots could hold soil in place, reduce erosion and stabilise shorelines around vulnerable coastal areas. At the time, the trees seemed like a useful solution for an island environment shaped by waves, storms and shifting sediment. More than a century later, that decision has produced a very different legacy. Red mangroves have spread across wetlands and estuaries, forming dense thickets that block waterways, alter water flow and crowd out native plants. They are now affecting habitats used by endangered Hawaiian waterbirds, including the aeʻo and ʻalae keʻokeʻo. As explained by the Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources and research supported by the USGS, the story is a reminder that an introduced species can appear beneficial at first while creating ecological problems that last for generations.Hawaii’s coastal wetlands have always been dynamic places. Freshwater streams meet the ocean, tides move through mudflats and lagoons, and native plants have adapted to changing salinity and water levels.These wetlands also provide feeding and nesting habitat for species found nowhere else on Earth.When red mangroves were introduced in 1902, they were viewed through a practical lens. They had dense root systems that could trap sediment and decrease erosion along the shoreline. On islands where land and infrastructure are concentrated along the coast, stabilising shorelines seemed like an obvious benefit. The trees were planted in areas where people wanted to hold soil in place and perhaps create more predictable coastal edges.The decision reflected a common approach to environmental management at the time. Species were often moved from one region to another because they were useful for forestry, agriculture, erosion control or landscaping. There was little thought about whether the introduced plants would escape from the sites where they were intended to grow, or how they would interact with native ecosystems that had evolved without them.Red mangroves are well adapted to coastal environments. Their propagules, which are elongated seed structures that can float, can travel through tidal channels and establish in suitable mud. Once rooted, the trees produce more propagules, allowing colonies to expand along shorelines, into estuaries and across wetland margins.Hawaii’s warm climate and sheltered coastal areas provided favourable conditions for the species. Over time the mangroves expanded far from where they were planted. Their roots formed dense networks in shallow water and their branches formed dense canopies above the wetland floor. These characteristics make mangroves successful in many parts of the world but in Hawaii, they may interfere with habitats that evolved without native mangrove forests. The trees alter the physical structure of wetlands, changing where water moves and where sediment settles. They can also transform open mudflats and shallow channels into closed, shaded thickets.The same qualities that made red mangroves attractive for erosion control became the source of their ecological impact. Their roots trap sediment, but too much sediment can fill waterways. Their shade protects the soil beneath them, but also reduces sunlight available to native wetland plants. Their dense growth creates cover, but may remove the open spaces required by native birds.Hawaii’s endangered waterbirds depend on a delicate mix of wetland conditions. Species such as the aeʻo, or Hawaiian stilt, and the ʻalae keʻokeʻo, or Hawaiian coot, need shallow water, mudflats and open vegetation for feeding, nesting and raising young. These birds forage in areas where they can see prey and move through the water easily.As red mangroves expand, they reduce the availability of these open habitats. Thick roots can limit bird movement within shallow channels. Dense plants can block their view and access to feeding grounds. Shifts in water depth and flow can also impact the invertebrates and small aquatic creatures that birds depend on for food. The effects are more than just a struggle for space. Wetlands are connected systems, and changes in one part of a wetland can impact conditions elsewhere. When mangrove roots trap sediment, they can gradually increase the wetland floor, change drainage patterns, and alter how tidal water enters and leaves. This can reduce the variety of habitats available to birds and other wildlife. For species already under pressure from habitat loss, predators, disease and human disturbance, the spread of an invasive tree adds another burden. Protecting the birds requires protecting the wetland conditions that support them.USGS research into mangrove biology explains why these tough trees handle different coastal environments so well. By studying how salinity and shade affect young seedlings, researchers can see how sprouts establish themselves and battle for space in wetlands. That’s important because mangroves don’t spread evenly along a coastline. Whether a seedling survives depends on the exact mix of salt, water, and sunlight, so some spots lead to rapid growth, while others stall out. Knowing those precise conditions gives land managers a real leg up. They can map out where mangroves are likely to take over next and figure out which cleanup or restoration tactics have the best chance of working. The research also shows why invasive species management requires more than just cutting down mature trees. If propagules remain in the water, or seedlings continue to establish, cleared areas can quickly become reinvaded. Effective restoration may require repeated monitoring, removal of new growth and the replanting of native species that can occupy the space.Scientific information about seedling growth can therefore guide practical decisions. It can help managers identify vulnerable spots, plan when to carry out removal work, and gage how environmental conditions affect recovery.The story of the red mangrove shows how environmental problems can build up slowly. Planting trees in 1902 might have looked like a sensible intervention with clear benefits. The people who introduced them could not have known that the species would spread through wetlands and create management challenges more than a century later. By 2026, the consequences are visible in waterways where roots obstruct flow and in wetlands where native birds have less open habitat. Removing the trees is costly, labour intensive and often controversial. Some people like mangroves because they provide habitat for some fish and wildlife, and shoreline protection. The challenge for Hawaii is to distinguish between the benefits the trees may offer in some settings and the damage they cause in ecosystems where they are invasive. The solution is not simply to reverse history. It is to understand where red mangroves are causing the greatest ecological harm and prioritise removal in those areas, especially wetlands that support endangered native species.The Hawaii Department of Land and Natural Resources has been working with conservation partners and local communities to address invasive mangroves. Management efforts may include cutting, uprooting, treating regrowth and restoring native wetland plants. Because the work often takes place in difficult terrain, crews must deal with deep mud, tidal water, dense roots and remote locations. Planning also requires careful attention to wildlife. Removal activities must avoid disturbing nesting birds and should be followed by monitoring to determine whether native vegetation returns. When mangroves are removed, in some places channels and mudflats may be opened up but restoration is not instant. The wetland needs time to recover and managers may need to manage invasive plants that will move into the newly opened space. Public buy-in is critical. Residents, farmers, fishers and conservation groups may have different views about mangrove removal. Explaining why the trees are invasive in Hawaii, and how their spread affects endangered birds, can help build support for targeted action.The history of Hawaii’s red mangroves offers a broader lesson about unintended consequences. People tend to try and solve one problem without understanding the system at work. Stabilizing a shoreline seems like a good thing to do but natural shoreline movement may be vital for wetland health. A tree that protects sediment in one setting may destroy open habitat in another. This does not mean every introduced species is harmful or every intervention should be avoided. It means decisions should be based on local ecology, long term monitoring and caution about irreversible changes. Island ecosystems are particularly vulnerable because they often contain species with small populations and limited places to escape new threats. The story also shows why early detection matters. Removing a few newly established plants is far easier than managing a forest that has spread across thousands of acres. Preventing introductions in the first place is usually less expensive and more effective than attempting to undo them decades later.For Hawaii’s endangered waterbirds, mangrove management is ultimately about restoring room to live. Open channels, shallow pools and mudflats may not look dramatic, but they provide the feeding and nesting conditions these birds need. Removing invasive red mangroves can help recover those spaces and reconnect wetlands that have become fragmented. The work will not erase the effects of 124 years overnight. Some wetlands may need years of monitoring and restoration before native plants and birds fully return. Yet each cleared channel and reopened mudflat can improve the resilience of the larger system. The red mangroves introduced in 1902 were planted as a tool to protect shorelines. Today, Hawaii faces the task of protecting its native wetlands from that same introduction. The experience is a reminder that nature rarely follows the simple plans people make for it, and that responsible stewardship sometimes means correcting decisions that once seemed helpful.plants water later birds mangroves waterways trees species waterbirds native wetlands red stabilize used wetland shorelinesIndian man on student visa in US sentenced to 30 months for defrauding Vietnam veteranVenkateswara Chagamreddy, an Indian man living in Texas on a student visa.

How was Chagamreddy caught?

US crackdown on elder fraud

He is expected to face removal proceedings from the US after completing his sentence.A federal jury convicted Chagamreddy in April 2026 of conspiring to defraud the elderly veteran. He will remain in custody pending his transfer to the US Bureau of Prisons.The case began in August 2025 when the elderly victim called a phone number he believed was Microsoft support. Here's how 9/11 changed the world in 25 ways:

The 9/11 attacks lasted hours, but their impact on wars, borders, technology and global politics has shaped the global since

25. The costs will continue long after the wars

Where we are, 25 years later

Twenty-five years ago America saw the darkest chapter in its history and the world hasn't been the same since.On September 11, 2001, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers seized four commercial aircraft and turned them into weapons. Two planes crashed into New York's World Trade Center, one struck the Pentagon and a fourth crashed into a field in Pennsylvania after passengers fought back. The attacks killed 2,977 people from 90 countries and changed the course of American foreign policy and global politics.The US invaded Afghanistan weeks later and Iraq less than two years after that. But the legacy of 9/11 reached far beyond those wars. Governments expanded surveillance and border controls. Airports became more heavily securitised. Intelligence agencies changed how they shared information. Drones transformed warfare, while the internet transformed terrorist recruitment. Islamophobia and debates over immigration intensified. America's global standing was damaged, while China's rise continued.The post-9/11 security state did more than give governments new powers; it changed expectations about privacy.The USA PATRIOT Act expanded US authorities' ability to access communications, financial records and other information in terrorism investigations. Later revelations about the collection of telephone and internet data showed how far surveillance had expanded. Other countries introduced or strengthened their own intelligence powers. The lasting shift was the growing acceptance that governments could collect and analyse enormous amounts of data in the name of preventing terrorism, even when most of the people being monitored were not suspected of any crime.Air travel changed almost overnight. Screening became more extensive, passenger information was checked against watchlists, and procedures such as shoe removal, liquid restrictions, enhanced searches and full-body scanning became familiar to travellers. The creation of the Transportation Security Administration in the US put airport screening under federal control.The US created the Department of Homeland Security in 2003, bringing together 22 federal departments and agencies. Its responsibilities stretched from airport and border security to emergency preparedness and protection of critical infrastructure. The change reflected a broader shift in how governments understood national security. Terrorism was no longer seen only as an overseas military or intelligence problem. Protecting the homeland became a permanent task involving airports, borders, transport systems, public spaces and local authorities.One of the clearest lessons of 9/11 was that important pieces of information existed before the attacks but were not effectively connected. US agencies subsequently changed how they shared intelligence, including through the creation of the Director of National Intelligence in 2004. Databases, watchlists and information-sharing systems became more integrated, while cooperation between intelligence and law-enforcement agencies expanded. Internationally, governments exchanged more information about suspected militants, travel and financial activity.Terrorism was increasingly treated as a financial problem as well as a military one. Governments pushed banks to identify customers, report suspicious transactions and trace money linked to extremist networks. The US Treasury gained powerful tools for freezing assets and imposing financial sanctions. These measures helped make terrorist financing harder, but they also transformed ordinary banking. International transfers, charity payments and opening accounts became subject to layers of identity and compliance checks.Within a month of the attacks, the US and its allies invaded Afghanistan to dismantle al-Qaeda and remove the Taliban government that had sheltered Osama bin Laden. The Taliban fell quickly, but the war did not. What began as a campaign against al-Qaeda became a two-decade effort involving counter-insurgency, nation-building and repeated Taliban offensives. The US withdrawal in 2021 was followed by the Taliban's rapid return to power. The episode became one of the defining questions of the post-9/11 era: what does victory look like in a war against a network rather than a conventional army?The 2003 invasion of Iraq widened the consequences of 9/11 far beyond Afghanistan. Saddam Hussein was removed, but the failure to find the stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction used to justify the invasion badly damaged trust in the war's rationale. Iraq then endured insurgency, sectarian violence and political instability. The conflict weakened existing regional structures and created space for armed groups to grow. The invasion became a turning point in Middle Eastern politics, demonstrating how quickly the removal of one government could produce consequences that spread far beyond the battlefield.The instability that followed the Iraq war helped create the conditions in which Islamic State emerged. By 2014, Isis controlled large areas of Iraq and Syria and proclaimed a caliphate. Its brutality was only one part of its power: it also became adept at online propaganda, recruitment and the use of social media. The group eventually lost its territorial state, but its rise showed how counter-terrorism campaigns could generate new security threats.The post-9/11 wars helped normalise a form of warfare in which a country could target suspected militants without sending large numbers of troops into battle. Armed drones became central to US operations in Pakistan, Yemen and Somalia, allowing strikes against targets thousands of kilometres from American bases. The technology reduced risks to soldiers and made some operations easier to conduct, but it also raised difficult questions about civilian casualties, intelligence failures and legal accountability.The overthrow of Saddam Hussein in 2003 removed one of Iran's most important regional rivals. Iraq's subsequent political instability created space for Iran to expand its influence through political allies and armed groups. The Syrian war later deepened this shift, drawing Iran, Russia, Turkey, Gulf states and the US into a complex regional struggle. The result was a Middle East in which power became more fragmented and non-state armed groups played a larger role.For the first time, NATO invoked Article 5, treating the 9/11 attacks as an attack on all its members. European allies and other countries joined the campaign in Afghanistan. Intelligence agencies expanded international cooperation, police forces created counter-terrorism units and governments coordinated watchlists and border controls. The result was a more interconnected security architecture. Yet the alliance was not immune to disagreement: controversies over detainees, drone strikes and the Iraq war exposed the limits of a global coalition built around a single threat.The US emerged from 9/11 with enormous international sympathy. That goodwill weakened as the wars dragged on and controversies over Guantanamo Bay, Abu Ghraib, interrogation practices and Iraq's weapons of mass destruction damaged Washington's credibility. Allies became more critical of American policy, while opponents used the wars to challenge US claims about democracy and human rights. Military power remained immense, but the post-9/11 period showed that even the world's most powerful country could struggle to turn military victories into political legitimacy and international trust.China's rise was already under way before 9/11. But the timing mattered. Beijing joined the World Trade Organisation in December 2001 and then experienced two decades of rapid economic expansion while Washington devoted enormous political, military and financial resources to Afghanistan, Iraq and the wider fight against terrorism. China's growing role in global trade and finance eventually translated into greater strategic influence. By the 2020s, the US increasingly viewed China, rather than jihadist terrorism, as its principal long-term strategic competitor. 9/11 did not cause China's rise, but it formed part of the geopolitical backdrop against which that rise accelerated.Counter-terrorism changed immigration and border control. Biometric identification, passenger databases, watchlists, more intensive visa checks and no-fly lists became standard features of travel in many countries. Measures originally designed to identify terrorism suspects increasingly became part of wider migration and border systems. For legitimate travellers, the change was often experienced as paperwork, interviews, fingerprints and longer checks. The deeper change was political: security became a central part of the debate over who should be allowed to enter, settle and move across borders.The attacks were carried out by 19 extremists, but suspicion and hostility often spread far beyond the perpetrators. In the US, reported anti-Muslim hate crimes rose sharply in 2001. Muslim and South Asian communities faced increased scrutiny, discrimination and hostility, including during travel and at workplaces. Across Western countries, terrorism became increasingly linked in political debate with immigration and Islam. The consequence was a lasting social divide: an attack carried out by a small extremist organisation contributed to a broader suspicion of millions of people who had no connection to it.The central political argument after 9/11 was simple but difficult: how much freedom should societies surrender in exchange for greater security? Expanded surveillance, detention without trial, interrogation programmes and broader police powers all became part of the debate. Supporters argued that exceptional threats required exceptional tools. Critics warned that temporary emergency measures could become permanent. Twenty-five years later, the argument remains unresolved.The detention facility at Guantanamo Bay became one of the most recognisable symbols of the post-9/11 security system. Hundreds of suspected enemy combatants were held there, often for years without conventional criminal trials. The prison generated international criticism over due process, interrogation and indefinite detention. Attempts to close it repeatedly stalled. Its importance goes beyond the number of prisoners who remain there. Guantanamo became shorthand for a broader question: can a democracy fight terrorism while maintaining the legal principles it claims to defend?The human consequences of the post-9/11 wars extended far beyond the countries where Western troops fought. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that more than 38 million people were displaced by wars in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, the Philippines, Libya and Syria. Millions crossed international borders, while many more were displaced within their own countries. The resulting refugee and migration pressures affected neighbouring states and reshaped political debates in Europe and elsewhere.The human cost of 9/11 did not end when the fires at Ground Zero were extinguished. Dust and toxic substances exposed responders, survivors and residents to long-term health risks. Thousands have since developed illnesses recognised as linked to the attacks and their aftermath. The James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act, passed in 2010 and later made permanent, created long-term support for affected responders and survivors.The physical site of the attacks was transformed into a place of mourning. The 9/11 Memorial opened in 2011, followed by the museum in 2014. Two reflecting pools occupy the footprints of the Twin Towers, with the names of the victims inscribed around them. Every year, families gather to read those names. After 25 years of arguments over war, surveillance and security, the memorial serves a different purpose: it brings the story back to the people who died. The remembrance is deliberately personal rather than political.The internet transformed the terrorist threat after 9/11. In 2001, extremist propaganda still depended heavily on traditional media. By the time ISIS emerged, militant groups could produce sophisticated videos, distribute propaganda instantly and reach potential recruits directly through social platforms and encrypted services. Governments consequently had to fight terrorism in a new environment where borders mattered less and information travelled globally in seconds. The battle was no longer only about finding people in physical networks; it was also about tracking ideas, recruitment and propaganda online.The post-9/11 security apparatus eventually produced a new question: who was watching the watchers? WikiLeaks' publication of classified US military and diplomatic documents, followed by Edward Snowden's disclosures in 2013 about mass electronic surveillance, exposed the extraordinary scale of government secrecy and data collection. The revelations showed how counter-terrorism programmes had expanded far beyond traditional spying on suspected militants. They triggered fierce debates over privacy, government transparency and the responsibilities of whistleblowers. Governments argued that such disclosures endangered national security; supporters said the public had a right to know what was being done in its name.The post-9/11 world changed not only government policy but also the stories people consumed. Films, television shows and video games increasingly revolved around terrorism, surveillance, soldiers, intelligence agencies and threats from within. Characters were often forced to make impossible choices between individual rights and public safety — mirroring arguments taking place in the real world. The culture of permanent threat became familiar entertainment. Over time, the fictional world of terrorist plots, security alerts and surveillance began to resemble the assumptions of everyday life.The post-9/11 era also changed how governments and political movements fought for influence. Terrorist groups used the internet for propaganda and recruitment, while states increasingly recognised that controlling information could be as important as controlling territory. Social media later allowed governments, political groups and foreign actors to reach millions of people directly, often without traditional media acting as a filter. Disinformation, manipulated narratives and online influence campaigns became tools of political competition. The result was a world in which a conflict could be fought not only with soldiers, missiles or sanctions, but with videos, social-media posts and competing versions of reality.The financial consequences of 9/11 did not end when troops left Afghanistan or the main fighting in Iraq subsided. Brown University's Costs of War project estimates that the US spent or committed about $8 trillion on post-9/11 wars through 2021–22, including future obligations for veterans. It estimates that healthcare and other costs for post-9/11 veterans could reach $2.2 trillion to $2.5 trillion by 2050. The final cost therefore cannot be measured only in military spending. It includes veterans' care, interest payments, lost lives, displacement and other consequences that will continue for decades. The wars may have ended, but their bills have not.Twenty-five years after 9/11, its legacy cannot be reduced to the destruction of the Twin Towers or the wars that followed. The attacks changed institutions, laws, borders, technology and the way governments understood security. They altered America's place in the world and reshaped politics far beyond its borders.The consequences were also measured in lives far from New York and Washington: soldiers killed, civilians displaced, communities divided and first responders who continued to suffer years after the smoke cleared.The most lasting legacy may be this: an event that lasted hours created assumptions about security, war and power that have lasted a quarter century.911 century americas darkest governments quarter wars terrorism 25 ways political war iraq intelligence changed day security world post911More than 1,000 volunteers built a four-bedroom house in just 50 hours; the unusual effort launched a 35-home community in San AntonioPC: San Antonio Express

From experiment to restoration

A reef begins to return

More than planting coral

When Hurricane Iris tore through southern Belize in 2001, it left more than a battered coastline behind. The storm severely damaged the region’s coral reefs, including those around Laughing Bird Caye. For marine biologist Lisa Carne, the destruction became the starting point for a restoration effort that has since helped put more than 100,000 corals back onto reefs across Belize, according to Fragments of Hope, the organisation she founded. The Commonwealth and UNDP have also documented the scale and impact of the project.Carne first travelled to southern Belize in 1994 after completing a biology degree in California. A year later, she moved to Belize and began working as a volunteer research assistant at the Smithsonian’s Carrie Bow Caye field station.Her work brought her into close contact with the country’s coral reefs and the growing threats they faced, including bleaching and disease. She later worked as a diving instructor, managed Glover’s Reef Marine Reserve and worked as a biologist with Friends of Nature, now the Southern Environmental Association.Then came Hurricane Iris.The Category 4 storm struck Belize in October 2001, causing extensive damage along the southern coast. At Laughing Bird Caye National Park, coral cover fell to less than 6%, according to a Commonwealth case study. But amid the devastation, Carne found something that suggested the reef might not be beyond saving.During a visit to San Pedro in northern Belize, she came across pieces of living elkhorn coral lying among seagrass. The fragments had broken away from larger colonies but were still alive. That observation led to a simple but then unconventional question: could broken coral be replanted on damaged reefs in much the same way trees are replanted on land?Carne began researching Belize’s Acropora corals, including elkhorn and staghorn coral. In 2006, she received a research grant from the Protected Areas Conservation Trust, allowing her to conduct restoration experiments at Laughing Bird Caye National Park.The first work involved transplanting elkhorn coral fragments to the damaged reef. The approach drew on coral nursery techniques pioneered by coral-restoration specialist Austin Bowden-Kerby. The work expanded in 2009, when Fragments of Hope established six underwater nursery sites near Placencia. Coral fragments were grown in nurseries before being transplanted onto degraded sections of reef.The organisation uses several nursery techniques, including metal A-frames, underwater tables and cement “cookies” that provide stable surfaces for coral fragments. Depending on the species, nursery-grown corals can later be moved to the reef once they have reached a suitable size.What started as a small experiment eventually became a large-scale restoration programme. Fragments of Hope says it now maintains more than 23 in-water coral nurseries and has outplanted more than 100,000 corals at more than 10 locations across Belize. Its restoration sites include Laughing Bird Caye National Park, Gladden Spit and Silk Cayes Marine Reserve, South Water Caye Marine Reserve and Turneffe Atoll Marine Reserve, as well as sites outside protected areas.At Laughing Bird Caye alone, the organisation says more than 49,000 nursery-grown coral fragments have been successfully outplanted. The site has become one of the project’s most closely documented examples of reef recovery. UNDP reported that coral cover at Laughing Bird Caye rose from less than 6% after Hurricane Iris to more than 50% by 2017. The restored reef has also provided habitat for fish and other marine life, demonstrating why branching Acropora corals are so important to Caribbean reef ecosystems.Fragments of Hope’s work has also grown beyond the physical act of putting coral back on the reef. The organisation works with local fishers, tour guides and other community members, training them to participate in coral nursery maintenance, outplanting and monitoring.The broader goal is to build reefs that can continue supporting marine life and coastal communities while facing recurring threats from hurricanes, warming seas, bleaching and disease.For Carne, the journey began with a landscape that appeared almost impossible to restore. Where will the $94 million go?

When will people actually move in?

According to Nevada officials, it represents the largest BLM land transaction in the Las Vegas Valley in more than two decades.The developers are planning Monument Hills as more than a collection of suburban housing tracts. The approved plans allocate space for residential neighbourhoods, commercial uses, schools, parks, trails and other public facilities. A tail that looks like a spider

Scientists wanted to see what was inside

The strange surprise inside the tail

The natural world is full of animals that use mimicry to survive, but few examples are as unusual as the spider-tailed horned viper. Native to Iran, this elusive snake has evolved a remarkable tail tip that resembles a spider, complete with a bulbous body and dangling, leg-like structures. The snake moves the strange appendage in a way that can attract birds close enough for it to strike. What looks like an elaborate spider from the outside, however, hides a much more ordinary structure inside. According to the Field Museum, scientists have now used X-ray computed tomography, or XCT, to examine the interior of the snake's unusual tail without damaging a scientifically important museum specimen. Their findings, published in The Anatomical Record, revealed that despite the extraordinary appearance of the tail, the vertebrae inside are surprisingly typical of vipers.The snake, scientifically known as Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, was formally described as a new species in 2006. Its common name, the spider-tailed horned viper, refers to the remarkable structure at the end of its tail. The appendage is not an actual spider. Instead, it is a specialised external structure that creates the appearance of one. When the snake moves the tail, the spider-like shape can become an attractive target for birds.A bird approaching what appears to be potential prey may come within striking distance, allowing the viper to turn the deception into a hunting opportunity.The species' unusual appearance was not immediately understood. A specimen collected in 1968 and later brought to the Field Museum was initially thought to have some kind of deformity at the end of its tail. It remained in the museum's collections for decades until another specimen with a similar tail was discovered in 2003, prompting scientists to reconsider the strange structure.The unusual tail eventually attracted the attention of Georgios Georgalis, a paleontologist and the first author of the new study. According to Field Museum, Georgalis was particularly interested in the viper's vertebrae because snake fossils often provide scientists with only individual bones, making it difficult to determine exactly what an ancient animal looked like. Researchers wondered whether the spider-like tail's dramatic appearance was reflected in the snake's skeleton. Georgalis noted that in some other snakes, including sand boas and rubber boas, vertebrae near the end of the tail can have unusual shapes. The team therefore wanted to know whether the spider-tailed horned viper had similarly distinctive bones.The Field Museum's new XCT laboratory provided a way to investigate that question without opening or damaging the specimen. XCT scanning works by collecting thousands of X-ray images and combining them to create a three-dimensional view of an object's internal structures. This was particularly valuable because the specimen in question is the holotype, the reference specimen used to establish the physical characteristics of the species.When the museum's XCT laboratory began operating in late 2024, the spider-tailed horned viper was among the first specimens scanned. Scientists expected the unusual exterior might be supported by equally unusual skeletal structures. Instead, the scans showed something much more ordinary. The vertebrae inside the tail were typical of most vipers. The dramatic spider-like appearance was an external feature rather than something reflected in the underlying bones. In other words, the snake's skeleton alone would not reveal that its tail could look like a spider or that the animal uses it to attract birds.The discovery also offers an important lesson for paleontologists. Fossilised skeletons can reveal valuable information about extinct animals, but they rarely preserve soft tissues and other external features. That means an animal could have looked dramatically different from what its bones alone suggest. For researchers, the spider-tailed horned viper demonstrates how much information can disappear from the fossil record. Its skeleton appears relatively ordinary, while its living body has evolved one of the most unusual hunting tools known among snakes. The study also highlights the continuing value of museum collections. A specimen collected decades ago and stored in a museum can become the focus of new research when technologies such as XCT scanning make it possible to examine it in ways that were previously impossible.unusual surprisingly spider normal inside grows snakes viper scanned xct museum scientists lure horned specimen spidertailed snake tailScotland’s first commercial wind farm recycled and reused 99.9% of materials from 26 old turbines, with blades turned into construction polymersRepresentative image

Scotland’s first commercial wind farm gets a new life

99.9% of old materials were recycled or reused

Old turbine blades became construction polymers

26 turbines replaced by 14 larger machines

A blueprint for future wind-farm repowering

Scotland’s first commercial wind farm has reached a major milestone in dealing with turbine waste after almost three decades of operation. Hagshaw Hill in South Lanarkshire, which began operating in 1995, was decommissioned and repowered with 14 newer turbines after its original 26 turbines were dismantled in 2023. A Mott MacDonald assessment commissioned by ScottishPower Renewables found that 79.5% of materials from the old turbines and associated components were recycled, while another 20.4% were reused, giving a combined recovery rate of 99.9%. The project also found a new use for one of the wind industry's more difficult waste streams, with all the old turbine blades processed by Northern Ireland-based Plaswire into polymer materials for construction and engineering applications.Hagshaw Hill began generating electricity in 1995 and became Scotland’s first commercial wind farm. Located in South Lanarkshire, the site operated for almost 30 years before its original turbines were dismantled in 2023 as part of a repowering project. The old installation had 26 turbines, while the replacement project uses 14 much larger and more powerful machines. The Scottish Government approved 14 turbines with a maximum tip height of 200 metres and a maximum generating capacity of 84MW.ScottishPower says the repowered project provides more than 79MW of capacity.The Mott MacDonald assessment commissioned by ScottishPower Renewables found that 79.5% of materials from the decommissioned turbines were recycled and 20.4% were reused. Together, the figures represent a 99.9% recycling and reuse rate. Reused components include equipment that has been retained for industry training as the wind sector prepares for more turbine decommissioning and repowering projects.The project also relied heavily on local businesses. ScottishPower says the majority of the recycling and reuse supply chain was located within 30 miles of Hagshaw Hill. At least 10 supply-chain companies in Scotland and elsewhere in the UK received contracts connected with the decommissioning work.One of the most notable parts of the project was the treatment of the turbine blades. Unlike metals such as steel, composite blades can be difficult to recycle because they contain layers of materials bonded together. At Hagshaw Hill, all the blades from the original turbines were recycled by Northern Ireland-based Plaswire.The company processed the blade material into its RX Polymer, which can be used in construction and engineering applications. The recycled material can replace products made from virgin plastics, timber and precast concrete. Potential applications include site fencing, marker posts, drainage components and other construction products.Plaswire's process involves processing composite blade material into smaller pieces before incorporating it into the recycled polymer. This gives the old blades a second industrial use instead of sending them for disposal.The Hagshaw Hill repowering project significantly increased the amount of electricity the site can generate. The original 26 turbines had a combined capacity of about 15.6MW. The new development has 14 turbines and more than 79MW of generating capacity, meaning the site's capacity has increased roughly fivefold while the number of turbines has almost halved.ScottishPower says the repowered wind farm can generate enough electricity to power the equivalent of around 57,000 homes. The approved development also includes provision for around 20MW of battery energy storage.The repowering means the established wind-farm site can continue generating renewable electricity with newer, more efficient technology rather than relying on the original turbines installed in the 1990s.Hagshaw Hill's transformation comes as older wind farms around Scotland and the wider UK approach the end of their original operating lives. The project demonstrates how decommissioning and repowering can be combined with large-scale material recovery.ScottishPower says around 1GW of its turbines are expected to come down over the next decade, creating a growing need for recycling and reuse solutions for components such as steel, electrical equipment and composite blades. Hagshaw Hill provides an example of how these materials can be redirected into new uses while newer turbines increase renewable-energy generation.The project has also brought greater benefits to nearby communities. The fund is around 26 times larger than the one associated with the original wind farm.Hagshaw Hill has therefore gone from Scotland's first commercial wind farm to an example of how an ageing renewable-energy site can be given a second life, with fewer and more powerful turbines producing substantially more electricity while almost all material from the old installation is recycled or reused.blades recycled materials old turned turbines polymers original project farm reused wind hill scotlandsIn 1999, Steven Spielberg and Kate Capshaw bought a 2.8-acre Los Angeles horse ranch for $5.75 million; 27 years later, their seven-bedroom equestrian estate with a 20,000-sq-ft riding arena is seekinIn 1999, filmmaker Steven Spielberg and his wife, Kate Capshaw, purchased a sprawling ranch in Los Angeles through their corporate entity, Texas Tart, for $5.75 million.
